title: Humans: A Monstrous History
description:
Surekha Davies's Humans: A Monstrous History reads the history of monster-making as a history of who gets to count as normal.

Davies traces how people have defined the human in relation to everything from apes to zombies, and how race, gender and nations were invented along the way. Her examples run from ancient gods and Frankenstein's monster to E.T. and generative AI. Her argument is that monster-making is about control. The University of California Press published it in February 2025 as a 336-page hardcover with ten color plates and forty black-and-white figures.

Davies is a British historian of science, art and ideas. Her first book, Renaissance Ethnography and the Invention of the Human, won the Morris D. Forkosch Prize and the Roland H. Bainton Prize. She has written essays and reviews for the Times Literary Supplement, Nature, Science and Aeon.

title: Harold's End
description:
JT LeRoy's Harold's End is a short, illustrated novella about a San Francisco street hustler, an older man, and a snail.

The narrator is Oliver, a youth on Polk Street feeding a heroin habit, who is taken in by a man named Larry. Larry provides shelter and drugs and takes an interest in Oliver's pet snail, Harold. The Last Gasp edition runs to 99 pages and is illustrated with eight watercolor paintings by the Australian artist Cherry Hood, each based on the story's character descriptions. Dave Eggers contributes an introduction. Last Gasp also issued signed copies, signed by LeRoy and Hood.

LeRoy's earlier books, Sarah and The Heart Is Deceitful Above All Things, were both international bestsellers, according to Last Gasp. Hood's watercolor of a boy holding a snail in a cup appears in miniature on the black cloth cover.

title: Zero: The Biography of a Dangerous Idea
description:
Charles Seife's Zero is a popular history of one number and the arguments it has set off in mathematics, philosophy, religion and physics.

Seife follows zero from its birth as an Eastern philosophical concept to its struggle for acceptance in Europe and its rise in the West. Along the way he covers the thinkers who tried to understand it, from Pythagoras and Newton to Heisenberg, and the clashes that pitted East against West and faith against reason. The book closes on zero in black holes, the Big Bang and the search for a theory of everything. This Penguin paperback is 256 pages.

Seife is a science journalist and a professor of journalism at New York University. Zero won the PEN/Martha Albrand Award for first nonfiction and was a New York Times Notable Book. His later books include Proofiness. He has written for the New York Times, Wired, New Scientist, Science, Scientific American and The Economist.

title: Paris, Capital of Modernity
description:
A collection of David Harvey's essays on Second Empire Paris, read as the place where nineteenth-century capitalist modernity took shape.

The book is arranged in three parts: Representations, Materializations and a Coda. Early chapters take up the myths of modernity and the body politic. The long middle section follows the city through space relations, credit and finance, rent, the state, labor, women's work, consumerism and spectacle on the boulevards. It reads the work of Balzac, Baudelaire and Zola alongside this material, and closes with the building of the Sacré-Coeur basilica. The volume is heavily illustrated and includes drawings, portraits and cartoons by Daumier.

Harvey is a British-American geographer and Marxist theorist, Distinguished Professor at the Graduate Center of the City University of New York, and long associated with urban political economy and the idea of the right to the city. Here his usual economic analysis is applied to a single city and a single period, with literature and caricature as evidence.

title: The Catwalk Cats
description:
A book of photographs and drawings in which two fashion-world figures portray their household of cats.

Grace Coddington and Didier Malige lived together for more than twenty years with a group of cats, and the book records that household through Malige's photographs and Coddington's drawings. The cats are named and characterised one by one, among them Henri, a catnip-addicted surfer, his sister Coco, and the Persian Bart. Coddington and Malige tell their working and private lives through what the cats see. Sally Singer wrote the introduction and Michael Roberts is credited as editor. It was published in 2006 by Edition 7L, the Steidl imprint.

Coddington is a Welsh former model and former creative director at large of American Vogue, known for large, elaborate and dramatic photographic shoots. Malige is a French hairstylist raised in Paris.

title: Paris versus New York: A Tally of Two Cities
description:
A book of paired graphic illustrations that set Paris against New York, one detail at a time, from a blog the author began while living in New York.

Each spread sets a small image and a short tagline from one city against its counterpart in the other, in graphic form. The book grew out of an online travel journal that Vahram Muratyan started in 2010 during a long stay in New York, written from the point of view of a Parisian wandering the city. The Penguin Books edition appeared in January 2012 and runs to 224 pages. A French edition was published by 10-18, and a later Penguin title, Paris Versus New York: The Complete Series of Two Cities, is listed under another ISBN.

Muratyan is a French visual storyteller and art director. After the blog drew wide attention he showed the series in print at colette in Paris and at The Standard in New York.

title: Benjamin Franklin's Autobiography
description:
Benjamin Franklin's account of his own life, written in four installments over nearly twenty years and left unfinished at his death, is among the best-known life stories in American letters.

The Autobiography begins as a letter to his son William, written in England in 1771. It covers his boyhood in Boston, his apprenticeship to his brother James, and his move to Philadelphia. Franklin resumed it in Paris in 1784, adding his plan for moral perfection through thirteen virtues. Further sections, written in 1788 and in the last months of his life, cover his almanac, his electrical experiments, and his mission to London for the Pennsylvania Assembly. It first appeared in French in 1791. This is the Everyman's Library edition, no. 316, from J.M. Dent & Sons of London with E.P. Dutton in New York.

Franklin (1706 to 1790) was a printer, the author of Poor Richard's Almanack, and a scientist. He was the first American ambassador to France and signed both the Declaration of Independence and the Constitution. Everyman's Library was founded in 1906 by J.M. Dent, with Ernest Rhys as editor, to put a wide collection of world literature in affordable pocket-sized hardcovers.

title: No Way Back 002: Better Ways Forward Through Music and Subculture Stories, 1979–1997
contributors: Steven Harvey (Original contributor (reprinted)); Steve Eichner (Original contributor (reprinted)); Sheryl Garratt (Original contributor (reprinted)); Jon Savage (Original contributor (reprinted)); Paul Morley (Original contributor (reprinted)); Eddie Otchere (Original contributor (reprinted)); Kodwo Eshun (Original contributor (reprinted))
description:
No Way Back 002 is the second issue of a printed magazine that reprints period journalism and photography on music, clubs and subculture from 1979 to 1997.

The issue gathers pieces from The Face, i-D, Time Out, Village Voice, Rolling Stone, Mixmag, The Observer and David Toop's Collusion. It also reproduces photographs and covers and spreads from the original titles. Steven Harvey's 1983 Collusion feature covers the New York disco underground. Steve Eichner photographed the club kids at The Limelight, Palladium, Tunnel and Club USA. Sheryl Garratt reported from Chicago for The Face in 1986, Jon Savage spent a night at Jive Turkey in Sheffield, and Kodwo Eshun wrote on jungle for i-D in 1994, with jungle images from Eddie Otchere. The editors add notes and playlists. It runs 208 pages at 165 × 240 mm and went on sale in April 2026.

The first issue, NWB001, covered 1977 to 1989. This one moves the span to 1979–1997 and keeps the focus on moments in dance music, hip-hop and pop, with parallel shifts in art, design and fashion. The publisher describes the material as culture recorded in the moment, before later interpretation settled over it. The issue carries ISSN 2977-8530 and no ISBN.

title: Top Shelf
description:
Top Shelf is a one-off limited-edition publication from The World of Interiors devoted to sex and erotica in design, issued alongside the magazine's body-themed September 2026 issue.

The 76-page volume at 165 × 222 mm sets images against four essays. The essays take up a museum's collection of sexually explicit objects, the use of the human body in decoration and design, the erotics of renovation, and the sexually explicit furniture associated with Catherine the Great. The pictures run from 19th-century brothel architecture to medieval pilgrim badges, contemporary film concept art and contested sculpture. The editors frame the project around the tension between revelation and concealment in domestic space, which is the parent magazine's long-standing subject.

The World of Interiors is a London magazine owned by Condé Nast. Emily Tobin is editor-in-chief and Ben Weaver is art director. The dating app Feeld sponsored Top Shelf, and the launch was held at Shreeji News in London. The cover uses an engraved sheet of nude figures in framed vignettes under the magazine's name.

title: Subliminal: How Your Unconscious Mind Rules Your Behavior
description:
Subliminal is a popular account of cognitive and social psychology by the physicist Leonard Mlodinow, arguing that much of what drives perception, memory and judgment happens outside conscious awareness.

Pantheon published the hardcover in 2012, at 260 pages. The chapters move from the brain's two tiers and the new science of the unconscious to how the senses and the mind together build a picture of reality, how memory works and fails, and how people read one another in social life. The book won the 2013 PEN/E.O. Wilson Literary Science Writing Award, and Vintage issued a 272-page paperback in February 2013.

Mlodinow holds a PhD in theoretical physics from UC Berkeley and taught at Caltech. He co-wrote The Grand Design and A Briefer History of Time with Stephen Hawking, and the cover of this book names his earlier bestseller The Drunkard's Walk. Subliminal applies the same explanatory habit to psychology.
